subject: California ground squirrel
title: A Squirrel Heats Up Its Tail to Scare Rattlesnakes. It Doesn't Bother for Other Snakes

scenes.text: This squirrel walks up to rattlesnakes and makes its tail hot. On purpose.
When a California ground squirrel finds a rattlesnake near its burrow, it waves its tail and pumps blood into it, warming it by several degrees.
Rattlesnakes hunt with heat sensing pits on their face. To the snake, that tail suddenly looks huge and hot.
Scientists at UC Davis built a robot squirrel with a heated tail. Snakes facing the hot tail stopped hunting and coiled up to defend themselves.
Against gopher snakes, which cannot see heat, the squirrels wave their tails but never warm them. They know which snake is watching.
Adults are also partly immune to the venom, and they chew shed rattlesnake skin to smell like the enemy. The snake came to hunt. It leaves rattled.

description:
California ground squirrels confronting a rattlesnake wave their tails and pump them full of warm blood, raising the tail temperature by several degrees. Rattlesnakes sense infrared through facial pits, so the hot, waving tail makes the squirrel look larger and more dangerous.
In a 2007 PNAS study, Aaron Rundus and colleagues at UC Davis used a robotic squirrel: with a heated tail, rattlesnakes shifted from hunting to defensive behaviour, coiling and rattling. Against gopher snakes, which lack heat pits, the squirrels wave their tails but do not heat them. Adult squirrels also have partial resistance to rattlesnake venom and chew shed snakeskin to mask their scent.
